1.4 — Movement I: Input, Direction, Vector

In a game, movement looks effortless. In code it is an algorithm, and today you build it: read the player's input → turn it into a distance → move the character by that distance. Three steps, one of them per frame. Every line is given to you below with an explanation of what it does — nothing here is a puzzle to solve on your own.

Where you are starting from. Open Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. It is a shell — a class with two empty methods. Your character has a Transform and nothing else: no physics body, no collider. Everything your character does from here on, you write. That is the whole design of this course.
In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I move an object in Unity?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

Move the character when I press the arrow keys. That is the whole feature — and as a single problem it is far too big to start typing.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Find out which way the player is pushingAsk the keyboard for two numbers: one for left/right, one for up/down. Each comes back between -1 and 1. Store them in fields on the class, so they survive the frame they were read in.Read: Input.GetAxis and the declare-vs-assign rule you met in 1.3, both in the quick reference.
  2. Turn those two numbers into one directionA pair of numbers is awkward to move by. Combine them into a single Vector2 — one value that means "this far in this direction", which is what the movement step wants.Read: Vector2, in the quick reference.
  3. Move the player by that direction, every frameOffset the position by direction x speed x the time since the last frame. Multiplying by that time is what keeps the speed in units per second rather than units per frame.Read: transform.Translate and Time.deltaTime, in the quick reference.

Three parts, and notice that only one of them is the part you would have thought of first. "Move the player" sounds like one action; it is a read, a build and an offset. Nearly every feature in this game splits the same way — something you find out, something you work out from it, and something you do with it.

The test for a finished split: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Move the player" cannot be looked up. "Get keyboard input as a number" can.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Last lesson you learned the difference between declaring a variable and assigning to it. Which of the three parts above is that rule doing the work in — and what would go wrong if you got it backwards?

In 1.3 you printed a number to the Console. What is the same about the numbers you read from the keyboard today, and what is different?

This is the first thing you have built that changes something every frame. Which method runs every frame, and which of your three parts belongs inside it?

Read the Docs ~12 min

You are about to write one of these into your code. Read all four before you choose — they are genuinely different tools, and the choice changes how the game feels.

Unity APIReturnsBehaviour
Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") float (−1.0 to 1.0) Smooth ramp. Gradually accelerates toward −1 or +1, then coasts back to 0 when you let go. Gives movement a little weight.
Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal") float (−1, 0, or 1) Instant snap. Exactly −1, 0 or 1 the moment a key changes, with no smoothing. Stops the instant you let go.
Input.GetKey(KeyCode.D) bool Binary state. True while the physical D key is held; false otherwise. Always the same key, on every keyboard.
transform.Translate(vector) void Offsets the position by a vector. A relative step: "move this far from wherever I am right now."

Notice that "Horizontal" and "Vertical" are quoted strings, not key names. They are virtual axes, defined in Edit → Project Settings → Input Manager. Open that window and read what each one is bound to — you may be surprised how much is wired up already.

Socratic: Evaluating Multiple Ways to Solve a Problem

  1. For a driving game, or a character with heavy momentum, which gives the better feel — GetAxis or GetAxisRaw? Why?
  2. For a precision grid puzzle, or a fast arcade game where you must stop on a dime, why might GetAxisRaw be better?
  3. What happens if a player wants to use the arrow keys, or a USB controller, instead of WASD? Why is asking for the virtual axis "Horizontal" more flexible than hardcoding KeyCode.D?
  4. You will use one of these today. Which one, and what does your choice cost you?
Build It With MeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I move an object in Unity?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. You will build two-axis movement — the kind you steer with WASD or the arrow keys — and every line of it is given and explained below.

Step 1Open the class and add the speed knob

PlayerController should already exist on the Player with two empty methods. The first thing it needs is a number that says how fast to move.

1using UnityEngine;23public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour4{5    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;
  1. 1Same as last lesson — gives you MonoBehaviour, Input, Vector2, Time and Transform.
  2. 3The class that is already attached to your Player. Do not rename it — Unity finds it by this name.
  3. 5How many units the player travels in one second. [SerializeField] exposes it in the Inspector so you can tune it live without touching code.

Step 2Declare the fields that remember the input

This is last lesson's rule doing real work. Read the two comments carefully — this exact step is where movement code usually goes wrong.

1    private float inputX;2    private float inputY;34    void Update()5    {
  1. 1Stores the left/right key direction as a number: -1 for left, 0 for nothing, 1 for right. It sits in the class body, so it belongs to the Player and survives from one frame to the next.
  2. 2The same thing for up/down: -1, 0, or 1.Why here and not inside Update()? If you declare inputX inside Update(), it is created fresh 60 times a second and thrown away each time. Nothing after that frame could ever see it. Declaring it here means Update() assigns to a variable that already exists — exactly the declare/assign split from 1.3.
  3. 4The method Unity calls every frame. All three of the remaining steps happen inside it.

Step 3Read the keyboard

Ask Unity what the player is pressing right now, and store the answer in the two fields you just declared.

1        inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");2        inputY = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");34        Vector2 movement = new Vector2(5            inputX * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime,6            inputY * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
  1. 1Reads the virtual axis called "Horizontal" and stores the result in inputX. Notice there is no float in front of it — the variable already exists, so this line only gives it a value.Writing float inputX = ... here instead would create a *second, temporary* variable that shadows the field, dies at the end of the frame, and leaves the real field untouched. That is the single most common bug in this lesson.
  2. 2The same read for up/down. The axis name in quotes must be spelled exactly "Vertical" — capitals matter, and a typo throws an error rather than failing quietly.
  3. 4Builds one value that holds both directions at once. This one is declared inside Update(), and that is correct — it is built from this frame's input and used two lines later. Nothing next frame needs it.
  4. 5The horizontal distance to travel this frame: direction × speed × how long the frame lasted. The commas matter — this is the first of two arguments.
  5. 6The vertical distance, same recipe. The closing ); finishes the Vector2 and the line.

Step 4Apply the movement

You now hold a displacement — "move this far from where I am." Hand it to the Transform.

1        transform.Translate(movement);2    }
  1. 1Offsets the Player's position by that displacement. transform is the Player's own position/rotation/scale, available on every GameObject without you declaring it.
  2. 2Closes Update(). One more } closes the class.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • float inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal"); written inside Update()

    You will seeThe character does not move, or jitters oddly. If another method tried to read inputX it would only ever see 0.

    Do thisDeclare private float inputX; in the class body and assign to it in Update() with inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal"); — no float on the second one. This is the declare/assign split from 1.3.

  • inputX * moveSpeed, with Time.deltaTime left off

    You will seeTapping a key for a fraction of a second flings the character across the entire map.

    Do thisMultiply by Time.deltaTime. Without it you are moving moveSpeed units per frame instead of per second, and there are ~60 frames in a second. It will also run at a different speed on a friend's computer.

  • Input.GetAxis("horizontal") in lowercase, or "Left/Right"

    You will seeAn error naming the axis, or the character simply refusing to move.

    Do thisThe axis is "Horizontal", with a capital H. Open Edit → Project Settings → Input Manager and read the real names — spelling is not forgiving here.

  • passing the vertical vector where the horizontal belongs

    You will seeA and D move the character up and down; W and S do nothing (or the reverse).

    Do thisThe first number inside new Vector2(...) is always horizontal (x), the second is always vertical (y).

  • nothing happens at all when you press Play

    You will seeNo movement, no errors. The Console is silent.

    Do thisCheck the script is actually attached to the Player in the Inspector, and that you saved the file. Unsaved changes do not reach Unity.

Check your work: the finished file

Compare this against your own file. Two things are worth checking closely: that inputX and inputY are declared up in the class body and only assigned inside Update(), and that both displacement lines are multiplied by Time.deltaTime.

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;

    private float inputX;
    private float inputY;

    void Update()
    {
        inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        inputY = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector2 movement = new Vector2(
            inputX * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime,
            inputY * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime);

        transform.Translate(movement);
    }
}
Test It, Then Break It ~22 min

Save your script, return to Unity, press Play, and hold WASD or the arrow keys. Your character should glide in all four directions. Now prove you know why.

Bug Hunt: Testing Assumptions

  1. Delete * Time.deltaTime from both displacement lines. What happens when you tap a direction key? Why does the character cross the entire map in a single frame?
  2. Set your moveSpeed knob to 0 in the Inspector while the game runs. What happens? Set it to 30. Describe the difference in one sentence.
  3. Swap the two lines inside new Vector2(...) — put the vertical calculation where the horizontal belongs, and vice versa. What does the character do now, and why?
  4. Now move your input declaration. Cut private float inputX; from the class body and put float inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal"); inside Update() instead. Does the character still move? Explain what happened to the variable, using the words declare and assign.
  5. Now the interesting one. Walk your character straight into a wall and keep pushing. What happens? Look back at the component list from 1.2 — what does the Player not have that would be needed to stop it?
Keep that last answer. Walking through walls is not a mistake in your code — transform.Translate moves your character by editing coordinates directly, so it never asks the physics engine anything. It will happily put you inside a wall, because nothing ever told it not to. Whether that matters depends entirely on the game you are making. In the next lesson you will compare every way Unity offers to move an object, and decide which one this game actually needs.

Tinker: Comparing input functions live

  1. Replace Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") with Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal"). Run the game. How does stopping feel compared to before? Which suits this game?
  2. Press W and D together to move diagonally. Does diagonal movement feel faster than moving in a straight line? (Hint: in 2D maths, what is the length of the hypotenuse of a right triangle with sides 1 and 1? What length do you actually want?)
  3. Add a second speed field — moveSpeedY — and use it on the vertical line only. Set it lower than the horizontal one. In top-down 2D games, why might a designer deliberately make vertical movement slightly slower?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • State the three sub-problems of character movement: input → vector → translation
  • Point at your own file and say which lines declare and which lines assign
  • Explain the difference between Input.GetAxis, Input.GetAxisRaw, and Input.GetKey
  • Explain why multiplying by Time.deltaTime is necessary
  • Find and tune your speed knob in the Inspector while the game runs
  • Explain why your character can walk through a wall right now
  • Commit and push your new movement code to your GitHub fork
